newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's industry fears future with strong lira.
newsitem.headline: Italy's industry fears future with strong lira.

text.p: A war of words between industry leaders and the government has laid bare fears that Italian business might be unable to compete against northern neighbours if the lira joins European economic and monetary union (EMU).

For the past 40 years businessmen have always known there was one thing they could count on to get them out of a tight spot -- a lira devaluation. That escape route will be sealed off for good if Italy joins a single European currency.

Underlying a growing sense of frustration among many businessmen is a belief that the centre-left government is not doing enough to create a level playing field for them to take on all comers in a currency union.
Once inside EMU, Italian companies fear they will carry a crushing burden if Italy's punitive tax system and creaking bureaucracy go unreformed.

"Italian industrialists see EMU coming down the road and they see that the government is not putting them in a position to compete. That is why they are getting angry," said Sergio Romano, a former diplomat and political commentator.

Giorgio Fossa, the pugnacious head of employers' federation Confindustria, launched a virulent attack on Prime Minister Romano Prodi's seven-month-old administration last week saying it risked being swept away unless it changed its policies.

The chairman of car group Fiat, Cesare Romiti, followed up with an even bleaker portrayal of Italy's plight as the government tightens the tax screws in a bid to meet stringent criteria for joining EMU.
"Italy is going through a tragic moment. The ruling class is poor in terms of personalities...and Italians realise they don't have a crumb of hope for the future," Romiti told a conference in Milan.
Italian businesses are already getting a taste of things to come as financial markets bet that Italy will scramble on board the EMU train and the lira firms against major currencies.

Shipments abroad of Italian goods boomed after the lira was forced out of the European exchange rate mechanism (ERM) in 1992 and lost more than one-third of its value against the German mark and the French franc.
The lira has since recovered and last month was readmitted to the ERM in what the government sees as a crucial step on the road to Italy joining EMU by 1999.

Fiat, Italy's biggest industrial employer, has been under growing pressure in recent months. Profits have slid as the Italian market fails to revive while the stronger lira has taken the competitive edge off exports.

"The mean of spirit maintain that, with the era of the big lira devaluations over, Fiat has to really fight against foreign competition and that it simply cannot cope," wrote Giuseppe Turani, an economic commentator, in Rome daily Repubblica.

The government's 1997 budget, designed to slash 62.5 trillion lire ($41 billion) off the public sector deficit, is long on taxes and conspicuously short on measures to curtail state welfare spending or high taxes on company profits.
Once the budget, now making its way through parliament, has been approved an informal halt may be called to hostilities between business leaders and the government, analysts say.

Economists at the employers' federation forecast the government will fail by a wide margin to meet a key target next year for qualifying for EMU -- cutting the ratio of the public deficit to gross domestic product (GDP) to three percent.

Prodi is expected to have to push through a supplementary budget early in 1997 to keep Italy's quest for EMU membership on course. Analysts believe that could trigger fresh clashes with the business community if he raises taxes once again.
"The tax burden here is without equal in the world," said Guidalberto Guidi, an Italian industrialist. "Prodi cannot continue to whip the entrepreneurial class with a constant string of tax bills."
